title: Do open permit records predict how long a permit and the build behind it take, better than each city's own averages?
lede: research programme: LightGBM quantile models beat the per-city, per-type empirical-quantile baseline on pinball loss in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells (2024 test year, Chicago, San Francisco, Austin); Chicago's tails are the exception
summary: An open research programme on duration forecasting from public building-permit feeds. Session 1 wrote the proposal (12 checked works, four falsifiable hypotheses, time-split evaluation with conformal intervals) and probed the feeds: Chicago has 851,778 rows, all issued, so it cannot show permits never issued; San Francisco has 1,297,657 rows with 750,188 completed; Austin has 2,382,939 rows with 2,184,191 completed. NYC DOB NOW is excluded until its licence is checked. Session 2 built the loader, schema, datasheets and a manifest (row counts match the probe) and found the median application-to-issue lag is 0 days in all three cities (p90 56, 81, 142), with SF and Austin build times at a median of about 105 days. Session 5 ran the reference-class baselines on the real feeds; session 6 (milestone 3) fitted LightGBM quantile models (q 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) and a same-day classifier, forward split with train to 2022 and early stopping on 2023, tested on 2024. The boosted model beats the baseline in 13 of 15 city/target/quantile cells by 2 to 36% (paired week-block bootstrap intervals exclude zero); in Chicago application-to-issue it wins at the median and loses at the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles. One test year, 3 seeds, fixed fast configuration, intervals not yet conformalised. Session 78 scored build time on Seattle test years old enough to be seen in full (2020 to 2022): folding demolition into alteration costs 1.7 to 2.5 days at the 0.9 quantile (95% intervals above zero), while complete-case scoring of a two-year window reverses that sign in two of three years, and inverse-probability-of-censoring weights recover only 10 to 40% of the gap because 5 to 8% of each cohort outlasts the window. The earlier fold gain is withdrawn as a censoring artefact; the transfer model's median gain stands. Session 79 ran the work-type class itself on the same mature cohorts: it lowers Seattle's build-time 0.9-quantile transfer loss by 3.2 to 6.3 days in every year (so the 2.2-day cost reported earlier was censoring too), and San Francisco's by 15.7 days, but raises Austin's by 15.3; folding demolition helps Austin by 2.0 days in 2021 (not in 2020, where it costs 1.8) and does nothing in San Francisco. Session 80 found the city signs hold in 2020 and 2022 (San Francisco +14.4 and +22.7 days, Austin −17.2 and −9.8) and traced both to which classes the source cities fill. Under permit type alone the sources have no rows in the held-out city's main classes; the work-type class fills San Francisco's alteration class (98% of its permits) with 271,672 source rows, but fills Austin's electrical, mechanical and plumbing classes (76% of its permits, 77 to 86% of the cost) with only 42 to 466 Seattle rows whose 0.9-quantile build times are 1.6 to 2.7 times Austin's own.
